newsitem.title: USA: New MagReTech magnesium plant to start up in July.
newsitem.headline: New MagReTech magnesium plant to start up in July.

text.p: The new MagReTech magnesium recycling plant in Ohio will start up in July and reach full capacity of 15,000 short tons a year within a couple of months, Tom Day, the company's general manager said.
The plant, which will recycle metal used to make auto components, is sizable by magnesium industry standards, and there are already plans to expand.
"We hope to start pouring metal in July," Day said. "We will certainly get up to full capacity as soon as possible."
MagReTech, part of Garfield Alloys Inc of Cleveland, has signed tolling contracts with scrap suppliers to operate the plant at close to capacity, Day said.
The company was still talking to other possible tolling customers and if enough additional contracts are signed, the plant would be expanded, Day added.
MagReTech already has blueprints to double capacity.
Robert VanFleteren, vice-president marketing at Dow Magnesium said MagReTech was being watched closely by the automotive industry which will be reassured by the added recycling capacity.

The light metal's biggest growth sector is in diecast components for vehicles, replacing aluminum or rivalling other materials, but some carmakers had expressed concern that the magnesium industry would have problems producing enough metal and be able to recycle it.

Howard Kaplan, vice president of sales and marketing at Magnesium Corp of America said of MagReTech: "I am a long-term proponent of an independent recycling industry, and encouraged by this. There is going to be more and more diecasting and this material has got to be recycled."
To alleviate these concerns, some carmakers have teamed up with existing or future magnesium production projects.
Kaplan declined to comment if MagCorp will toll some scrap at MagReTech.
Hydro Magnesium, part of Norway's Norsk Hydro, is expanding its Becancour plant in Canada which was due to add recycling capacity later this year.

Meanwhile producers are more optimistic about market prices, especially in the wake of last week's International Magnesium Association figures which showed stocks falling, first quarter production lower, but shipments rocketing to their best quarterly level ever.
VanFleteren said Dow has no immediate plans to hike U.S. prices.
MagCorp's Kaplan said demand has been strong and supply tighter.
"There is obviously some trend to a firming of prices and perhaps some increases," Kaplan said.
